content.audition.screen-test.check.0.en: You came dressed for the part.

content.audition.screen-test.check.1.en: You and your scene partner already found your rhythm.

content.audition.screen-test.check.2.en: You already know your way around a soundstage.

content.audition.screen-test.category.in.en: Why is this character in the room?

content.audition.screen-test.category.te.en: What do you lean on going in?

content.audition.screen-test.option.tech.en: The character work from Method Study.
Reading the room before you commit.

content.audition.screen-test.category.de.en: How do you deliver the line?

content.audition.screen-test.option.deli.en: Play it big for the back row.

content.audition.screen-test.category.bl.en: How do you use the space?

content.audition.screen-test.option.bloc.en: Claim more of the space than you were given.
Stay planted and play it safe.

content.audition.screen-test.category.im.en: The scene leaves an opening. Do you take it?

content.audition.screen-test.option.impr.en: Improvise big and hope it lands.

content.audition.screen-test.category.ad.en: The reader changes the cue on you. What do you do?

content.audition.lookout-first-day.check.en: You came to the set in your fitted costume.
You learned your three lines on the way over.
You and the wardrobe mistress thought about how the costume would move on camera.
You have a fourth line to land, and you have been practicing it.

content.audition.lookout-first-day.categ.en: Why does the Lookout warn the heroine?

content.audition.lookout-first-day.optio.en: Because she has spent a lifetime reading danger.
Because she is trying to make up for something.
Because it is your one chance to be noticed.

content.audition.lookout-first-day.categ.en: How do you deliver your three lines?

content.audition.lookout-first-day.optio.en: Low and quick, like someone who does not want to be heard.
Over your shoulder, on the move.
Pitched to the back of the soundstage.

content.audition.lookout-first-day.categ.en: The chalk marks put you at the edge of the crowd. What do you do with them?

content.audition.lookout-first-day.optio.en: Hit your mark and hold it.
Drift a half-step toward the lens.

content.audition.lookout-first-day.categ.en: The leading man fumbles his cue and the stuck prop crate will not budge. Do you take the opening?

content.audition.lookout-first-day.optio.en: Stay in the script and let the director sort it.
Improvise a line that covers for him.
Improvise big and hope it lands.

content.audition.lookout-first-day.categ.en: The director shouts for a second take with the crate still jammed. What do you do?

content.audition.lookout-first-day.optio.en: Take the blame for the crate and keep your place.
Quietly work the crate loose between takes.
Freeze until someone tells you what to do.

content.dialogue.casting-office-intro.ro.en: "Appointment, photograph, or miracle?" she asks, barely glancing up.
You mentioned a screen test. (-10 Energy)
Ask what the casting directors actually watch for. (-10 Energy)

content.dialogue.casting-office-intro.po.en: "They watch the hands, then the eyes, then whether you flinch when the light comes on," she says, stamping a folder without looking up. "Nobody tells you that. You did not hear it from me."

content.dialogue.casting-office-intro.sc.en: "Stage 4, dress in the dress. They’re waiting on you." She slides a dog-eared script across the counter.

content.dialogue.casting-office-intro.ph.en: "Not bad. Can you read for us Tuesday?"
Mention a contact on the lot.
Any word on the audition? (-10 Energy)
Ask if she can slot you in earlier.
Mention you have already been through one callback.
Show her the studio headshot from your last callback.

content.dialogue.casting-office-intro.mi.en: "Everyone wants a miracle. Come back with a photograph."
Remind her you already showed one.

content.dialogue.casting-office-intro.fa.en: "Oh — well, that changes things. Tuesday, front of the line."
"You landed it? Good. Keep that up and we’ll talk about the next one."
"Don’t make me regret this. Monday, then — first thing."

content.dialogue.casting-office-intro.c2.en: Clerk
For the first time since you walked in, the clerk looks up from her folder. "Monarch has been ringing this desk all morning," she says. "Sit. Don't touch anything."
Ask what Monarch made of your screen test.
Ask what Monarch made of your screen test.
Ask what Monarch made of your screen test.
Ask what Monarch made of your screen test.
Talk about something else.
Step back outside.
Clerk

"The assistant director watched your test twice," the clerk says, and something that is almost a smile crosses her face. "The Lookout, harbor market, three lines, and a fourth they wrote in after the dailies. Monarch wants you."
Take the part, and the fourth line.
Clerk
"They liked it. They also had questions," the clerk says, in the voice of someone who has learned not to say more. "The Lookout, three lines. The part is yours; the questions can wait."
Take the part as offered.
Charm her into one more line.
Joke your way to one more line.
Ask for one more line anyway.
Clerk

"You weren't what they were testing for," the clerk says. "But the casting director saw something, and there is a small part going: the Lookout, harbor market, three lines and a pickpocket's cap. Take it before somebody else sees what he saw."
Take the part as offered.
Charm her into one more line.
Joke your way to one more line.
Ask for one more line anyway.
Clerk
"It wasn't your best day," the clerk says, not unkindly. "But the assistant director argued for you, and the Lookout is still unfilled. Three lines. Don't make me regret this."
Take the part as offered.
Charm her into one more line.
Joke your way to one more line.
Ask for one more line anyway.
Clerk

She slides three pencilled pages across the counter. "Your sides. The Lookout warns the heroine in the harbor market, and then she runs. Take them to the wardrobe mistress at The Silver Thimble, and the extras corral will give you a call time."
Take the pages and thank her.
Clerk

She looks at you for a long moment, then pulls a pencil from her hair and scrawls a line at the bottom of the last page. "A fourth line. Don't let it go to your head." She slides the pages across. "Wardrobe at The Silver Thimble, then the extras corral for a call time."
Take the pages, and the extra line.
Clerk

"No," she says, flatly, and the pencil goes back in her hair. "Three lines is three lines." She slides the pages across anyway. "Wardrobe at The Silver Thimble, then the extras corral for a call time. Next time ask nicer, or ask later."
Take the pages and let it go.

content.dialogue.sunset-diner-intro.root.en: "Coffee, doll? You look like you could use it," she says, already reaching for the pot.

content.dialogue.sunset-diner-intro.sett.en: "So, what brings a face like yours to this end of the Boulevard?"
What is the real story on this town? (-10 Energy)
Read the room, then ask about the gossip column.
Ask how she ended up behind this counter. (-10 Energy)

content.dialogue.sunset-diner-intro.stor.en: "Came out from Ohio with a suitcase and a screen test that never happened," she says, wiping the counter in slow circles. "Turns out everybody in this town eats. Some of them tip like they remember being hungry."
Leave a little extra on the counter.

content.dialogue.sunset-diner-intro.goss.en: "Ask around enough and you will hear it all — who is bankable, who is trouble, and who is both."

content.dialogue.sunset-diner-intro.c2-r.en: "Well, if it isn't the picture person," the counter girl says, already sliding over a slice of pie nobody ordered. "Sit. Eat. The pie is on the house until the day you're famous enough to pay for it twice."
Stay after close and help count the tips.
Stay after close and help count the tips.

content.dialogue.sunset-diner-intro.c2-e.en: The last customer is gone and the chairs are up on the tables, and she is sitting on the counter with her shoes off, counting a coffee can of coins into piles. "Tips," she says. "Half of it is from people who'll be on a poster by Christmas, and the other half is from people who want to be." She nudges a pile toward you. "Do you ever wonder which you are?"
Say that you wonder every single day, and that you are glad of the pie. (-10 Energy)
Say you intend to be on the poster, and tip accordingly. (-10 Energy)
Say you are too tired tonight, and come back another evening.

She stops counting. "Well," she says, and for once there is no joke after it. "The pie is a good thing to be glad of." She scoops the coins into the can and swings her feet. "Whatever you are, you'll always have a stool here. I mean that. It's the only promise I make."
Take the stool, and the promise.
She laughs and pockets the coin you tip, but the laugh is a beat late. "Sure. Poster. Don't forget the diner." She starts stacking the cups, faster than she needs to. "I mean it as a joke. Mostly."

content.dialogue.boarding-house-intro.ro.en: "Rent's due Friday, same as always," she says, not looking up from her ledger.
Here — this week, paid in full.
Could I get a few more days?

content.dialogue.boarding-house-intro.se.en: "Just so we are clear where we stand," she says, setting down her pen.
I am good for it — steady work is coming. (-10 Energy)
Show her the callback slip from your last audition. (-10 Energy)
Ask about the photographs on her wall. (-10 Energy)

content.dialogue.boarding-house-intro.ph.en: "Every one of them slept in your room once," she says, tapping a frame of a young man in a borrowed tuxedo. "Two got a contract. One got a husband. The rest went home and swear they never wanted it." She turns the ledger a quarter-inch straighter. "Rent is due Friday, all the same."

content.dialogue.boarding-house-intro.c2.en: The landlady looks up from her ledger, and then, very deliberately, at the call sheet sticking out of your pocket. "Well," she says. "Look at that. Rent's still due Friday, but I'll allow myself to be proud for ten minutes."
Ask whether she has anything fit for an evening out.

"The Hollywood Bowl?" She puts down her pen, which she does for nothing. "Well. There's a good wool jacket in the hall trunk that belonged to a boarder who left in the middle of the night, owing me. And a hamper in the pantry, if someone were to chip in for a chicken." She raises an eyebrow. "Hold still. I'll need to take in the shoulders."
Chip in $10 for the chicken. (-10 Energy)
Tell her you'll owe her one. (-10 Energy)

She pins the shoulders with a brisk, practiced hand and, when she is done, steps back and does something she does not do: she smooths your lapel. "There. Take the hamper. Eat the chicken while it's warm, and for pity's sake, enjoy yourself."
Thank her, and take the hamper.

"You owe me one," she agrees, and writes something in her ledger that is probably not rent. The jacket is a little large and a great deal better than anything you have, and when she takes in the shoulders, her hands are surprisingly gentle. "Go. Enjoy yourself. And come back and tell me every word."
Promise to tell her every word.

content.dialogue.backlot-gate-intro.root.en: "Well, look who else got called back," she says, looking you up and down.
Look her up and down right back.
Same casting call, huh? Small town.

content.dialogue.backlot-gate-intro.sizi.en: "Let's see who's still standing after the next round of cuts," she says, but it sounds almost like a dare.
May the best actress win. (-10 Energy)
Careful — I don't lose easily. (-10 Energy)
Ask how her own audition went. (-10 Energy)

content.dialogue.backlot-gate-intro.audi.en: "They liked me. They always like me," she says, then looks away. "That is the trouble. Liked is not the same as chosen." A beat, and the smile is back. "Do not repeat that."

content.dialogue.backlot-gate-intro.c2-r.en: The rival is perched on the low wall by the gate, swinging one foot, a copy of the call sheet folded small in her fist. "So you're the new name on the Lookout," she says. "I'm not sorry to see a rival. I'm just not sure you are one."
Spend an evening on the lot with the rival.
Spend an evening on the lot with the rival.

content.dialogue.backlot-gate-intro.c2-d.en: "Small parts open big doors in this town," she says, "and then they close them behind you. Everyone on that lot is going to be very kind to you this month. I'd think about why." She slides off the wall. "I'm not telling you for your sake. I'd like you to be good, so that when I beat you, it counts."
Tell her you earned that call sheet, and you will keep it. (-10 Energy)
Tell her you were just about to say the same. (-10 Energy)
Offer her half your sandwich, and a truce. (-10 Energy)
Notice that she has not once looked at the call sheet. She is looking at the gate. (-10 Energy)

She studies you for a long moment, the way a card player studies a hand, and her mouth twitches. "All right," she says. "We'll see how long you hold it." She hops down from the wall. "I'm going to be watching, you know. Closely."
"Oh, I like you," she says, and it is not entirely a compliment. "That makes it so much more fun when I win." She salutes with the call sheet. "May the best name on the marquee win."

She looks at the sandwich, and then at you, and a laugh escapes her before she can stop it. "Half?" She takes it, and the bite is considered. "A truce. Fine. But it's only until one of us is on a marquee, and then I'm afraid it's every woman for herself." She looks briefly, startlingly shy. "Thank you. Nobody shares anything on this lot."
Finish your half of the sandwich.

She goes very still. "You noticed that," she says, softly. "I've been through that gate eleven times, and every time, somebody at the booth tells me it's the wrong day. I don't want your part. I want the other side of that gate." She exhales. "Nobody's ever noticed. Don't tell anyone."

content.dialogue.backlot-gate-intro.c2-e.en: The lot is empty at dusk, and she is rehearsing a speech to the painted wall of a soundstage, hands pressed flat to the plaster. She stops when she hears you. "Don't laugh," she says. "Everyone laughs. The voice in my head is much meaner than you could be." She steps aside. "Take the other half. Give me something to push against."
Read the other half honestly, and tell her what moved you. (-10 Energy)
Play it for laughs, and see if she can stay in character. (-10 Energy)
Say you are too tired tonight, and come back another evening.

She does not laugh. She goes through the speech from the top, and this time her voice does not shake, and when it ends there is a silence that does not need filling. "That's the first time that's worked," she says, at last. "I hate that it was you." But she is smiling. "Come back tomorrow, and I'll hate it again."

She plays along for nearly a minute, and then her face closes. "I wasn't asking for a joke," she says. "I was asking for a scene partner." She smooths her skirt and turns her face to the wall. "Another time. Perhaps."

content.dialogue.extras-corral-intro.roo.en: "Name?" he snaps, pen already hovering over the sign-in sheet. "Corral fills up fast — I do not have all morning."
Give your name and step back to wait.
Apologize — traffic on the Boulevard held you up.

content.dialogue.extras-corral-intro.che.en: "You're on the list," he says, already scanning past you toward the corral. "Stay behind the rope until someone waves you onto the set."
Ask what today's call actually needs from the extras. (-10 Energy)
Mention the callback slip from the casting office. (-10 Energy)
Ask how an extra gets noticed on a set this size. (-10 Energy)
Say nothing and wait for the wave-in.

content.dialogue.extras-corral-intro.not.en: "Hit your mark, hold your mark, and never look at the camera," he says, without lifting his pen. "Extras who do that get remembered. Extras who wave get replaced." He glances up, just once. "Take that free."
Take it to heart and get back behind the rope.

content.dialogue.extras-corral-intro.c2-.en: The assistant director is pinning call sheets to the corral board with a thumbtack in his teeth. "The Lookout," he says around it. "Good. I was hoping it would be someone who shows up."
Ask for your call time. (-10 Energy)
Join the veteran extra at the end of the bench.

"Soundstage, seven sharp, harbor-market set," he says, tearing a sheet off the board and pressing a day-rate advance into your hand. "Costume on, lines in your head, and don't talk to the camera operator. He bites." He pauses. "Good luck. The Lookout is a small part. Small parts are how I got started."

The old hand who taught you which end of a crowd scene to stand in is leaning on a barrel, working a crossword in pencil. "Kid," he says, without looking up, "I've got two tickets to the Hollywood Bowl and a friend who plays there summers. Somebody I want you to see. A good suit, a free evening, and nobody's business but ours."
Let me see how the week goes.

"Good." He tucks the pencil behind his ear and, for once, the crossword stays unfilled. "Ask the landlady for something that fits. Wear shoes you can stand in. And if I get a little sentimental, humor an old man."
"Tickets keep," he says, and goes back to his crossword. "People don't. Don't take too long."

content.dialogue.soundstage-intro.root.t.en: "You're covering my mark today?" she asks, flipping through her sides. "Let's at least get through it once before they roll film."

content.dialogue.soundstage-intro.root.c.en: Offer to run the scene twice before the crew is ready.
Play it too big, daring her to match you.

content.dialogue.soundstage-intro.settle.en: "Places in five," the assistant director calls from off camera. "You've got until then to find it," she says, script still in hand.
Play it exactly as blocked — no surprises. (-10 Energy)
Dig into what your characters actually want from each other. (-10 Energy)
Tell her you could get used to rehearsing with her. (-10 Energy)
Ask about her first role. (-10 Energy)

content.dialogue.soundstage-intro.first-.en: "A corpse in a two-reel comedy," she laughs. "Eleven takes, and the director told me I had a wonderful stillness." She lowers her sides. "The trick is that you never stop acting, even lying down."
Take the tip and return to your mark.

content.dialogue.soundstage-intro.c2-roo.en: The soundstage is a cathedral of cables, canvas and painted harbor. Somewhere above the rigging, the assistant director is calling names through a megaphone, and yours is on the list.
Ask for another go at the scene.
Return the wave of the glossy man by the cable trunks.
Spend an evening with the scene partner, running lines.
Spend an evening with the scene partner, running lines.
Spend an evening with the leading man.
Spend an evening with the leading man.

content.dialogue.soundstage-intro.c2-set.en: "You're the Lookout," the assistant director says, steering you onto a chalk mark by the elbow. "Three lines. Then the heroine runs, the leading man chases, and you flatten yourself against that crate. Don't look at the lens. Don't look at me. Places!" The crate, you notice, has been nailed down by someone in a great hurry.
Take your place on the mark.

content.dialogue.soundstage-intro.c2-day.en: "That's a wrap on the harbor market!" The assistant director claps his clipboard shut. "Your name is on the call sheet, which in this business is what we call a credit." The leading man gives you a two-fingered salute across the set, and a glossy man in a gray suit scribbles something in a notebook, smiling at you with every tooth.
Walk off the set with your head high.

"That's a wrap, and it could have been worse," the assistant director says, and thumps your shoulder. "Everyone has a first day. Mine involved a horse." Your name is on the call sheet all the same, and a glossy man in a gray suit is watching you from the cable trunks as though you were more interesting than you feel.
Walk off the set, a little wiser.

content.dialogue.soundstage-intro.c2-pik.en: Publicity Chief

"A new face on my set should never have to worry about their image," the glossy man says, producing a cream card from nowhere. "Newcomers worry about the wrong things: the lighting, the lines. I worry about the right ones, which is what people say about you before you open your mouth." Behind him, in the window above the stage, a silver-haired man stands very still, watching the floor. "The studio's owner likes to know who's new," he adds. "I like to make that easy for him."
Accept: let him look after your image.
Accept, and ask for the photographer's fee up front.
Ask what it will cost.
Refuse, politely.
Say you would rather do business with the newsman at The Klieg Light.
Publicity Chief

"Cost?" He laughs, and it is the first thing about him that looks entirely real. "Nothing at all. Today." He lets that sit between you. "You're sharp. I like sharp. Sharp people remember a favor, and the people who remember them are the ones who get on in this town."
Accept, with your eyes open.
Refuse, and say that you will remember he offered.
Publicity Chief

"Splendid." The card changes hands, and the glossy man's smile never quite changes with it. "Anything you need, just say. A photographer, a column inch, a quiet word with the right person. It's all small, and it's all on the house." He is already walking away. "Nothing in this town is free, of course, but I'm so very flexible about when it's due."
Pocket the card.
Publicity Chief
"A pity, and a wise one," he says, with exactly the same smile. "Keep the card, if you like. People change their minds. I do so enjoy being there when they do."
Leave the card where it is.
Publicity Chief

For half a second the glossy man stops smiling. Then he finds it again. "The Klieg Light. Of course. They do so love a trade." He tips an imaginary hat. "Do mention me to him. He'll know who you mean."
Watch him go.

content.dialogue.soundstage-intro.c2-eve.en: Scene Partner

The harbor set is dark, and she is in a canvas chair in a pool of work light, mending the sleeve of her heroine's blouse with a very small needle. "Sit," she says, patting the next chair. "I've been told we're friends now. I'd like to find out if that is true, preferably without a script."
Admit that the part scared you more than you let anyone see. (-10 Energy)
Keep it light, and do your best impression of the director. (-10 Energy)
Say you are too tired tonight, and come back another evening.
Scene Partner

"Everyone is scared," she says, quietly. "The ones who say they aren't are lying, or they're the director." She smiles at you, and for a minute there is no set, no studio, no schedule, only the two of you and a very small needle. "Thank you for telling me. I don't get told things."
Say goodnight.
Scene Partner

Your impression is, you are told, uncannily accurate, and she laughs until she has to put the needle down. But somewhere in the laughing, she goes quiet, and looks at you as though she had expected something else. "You do that very well," she says. "Making a joke. I wonder what you'd say if you didn't."
Say goodnight, a little thoughtfully.
Leading Man

The leading man is sitting on an apple box in the wings, taping his knuckles out of habit and gazing at nothing. "Stunt rider, before this," he says, when he notices you. "Nobody ever told me you had to talk and fall off a horse at the same time. I keep waiting for someone to notice I'm not a real actor." He looks up. "You did well today. How'd you do it?"
Tell him the truth: nobody feels like a real actor, not for years. (-10 Energy)
Tell him it is easy: you just pretend to be someone who isn't scared. (-10 Energy)
Say you are too tired tonight, and come back another evening.
Leading Man

He laughs, a real, startled laugh, and the tape stops mid-wrap. "Years. Good grief. I'd have signed for months." He studies you a moment, and then lets out a long breath. "Thank you. That helped more than a pat on the back would have. Will you do me the favor of running a scene with me tomorrow? Just so I'm not on my own."
Say you will.
Leading Man

"Pretend not to be scared," he repeats, slowly, and the smile he gives you is a polite one. "I've tried that. It works until someone says action." He stands, brushing off his knees, and the moment closes like a stage door. "Well. Goodnight. See you on the lot."
Wish him goodnight.

content.dialogue.silver-thimble-intro.ro.en: "Mind the pins, and keep your hands off the silk," she says, a yellow tape measure trailing from her neck. "Half of Monarch's call sheet is hanging in this shop, and every seam on it is mine."
Admire the swashbuckler's coat on the rack.
Ask whether she has a minute to size up a newcomer.
Show her the callback slip and ask for the proper fitting. (-10 Energy)

content.dialogue.silver-thimble-intro.pr.en: "A callback, and you remembered to come back," she says, pins already between her lips. "Arms out. Now we are talking about a costume that will make a director believe the rest of you." She chalks a line down your shoulder and, for the first time, almost smiles.
Stand very still and let her work.

content.dialogue.silver-thimble-intro.co.en: "The Corsair's Daughter," she says, smoothing a sleeve. "Forty yards of braid, and not one of those pirates can sit down in it. Ask me how I know."
Ask whether she could spare a minute for you, too.
Let her get back to the braid.

content.dialogue.silver-thimble-intro.fi.en: "Chin level, shoulders down, and do not breathe in," she says, chalk already moving. "A costume that fits is worth more to a career than a good headshot. Come back when you have a callback."
Thank her and promise to come back.

content.dialogue.silver-thimble-intro.c2.en: The wardrobe mistress peers at you over a pincushion strapped to her wrist. "Monarch sent your measurements ahead. Stand on the box. And stop looking at the door; the harbor market isn't going anywhere."

"Black photographs gray, white blooms, and a stripe will crawl on film if you let it," she mutters through a mouthful of pins. "So. The Lookout. A pickpocket in a harbor market. Do you want to be seen, to move, or to blend in?"
Be seen: a bright sash and a cap with a feather. (-10 Energy)
Move: nothing that will snag or crawl on film. (-10 Energy)
Ask how each layer will photograph, and plan the costume around the lens. (-10 Energy)
Blend in: something off the rack that has been on a hundred extras. (-10 Energy)
She stabs a last pin into the sash and steps back, squinting. "The camera will find you in that, for better or worse. Mostly better. Don't blame me if the director tells you to tone it down."

She nods slowly, the way someone does when a customer says the right thing without being told. "Good. Nothing to snag, nothing to crawl. You'll look like you grew up in that waistcoat." She starts pulling the pins. "Hold still."
"Third pickpocket this month," she sighs, taking in the seams the previous wearers let out. "It'll do. But you owe me one, and I don't mean the rental fee."

content.dialogue.klieg-light-intro.root..en: "Fresh face, no entourage, suitcase still on the shoulder," he says, notebook already raised. "Give me something I can print, and I'll owe you one."
Give him a harmless bit of color about your arrival.
Ask what he has heard about Monarch's casting.
Give him the story of your first day on set. (-10 Energy)
Ask him to hold the story until it is official. (-10 Energy)
Smile and say you have nothing to print.

content.dialogue.klieg-light-intro.tip-r.en: "Wholesome. My editor will hate it," he grins, scribbling. "But a name in print is a name people remember. Remember who put it there."
Tip your hat and head out.

content.dialogue.klieg-light-intro.gossi.en: "Monarch's casting is a revolving door, and Sunset Casting Exchange holds the key," he says, lowering his voice. "Be early and be reliable, and they forget you're new. Be a story, and I'll be the one who tells it."

content.dialogue.klieg-light-intro.print.en: "Cleared for the Monarch call, and still smiling? Readers will eat that with a spoon," he says, already writing. "Front of the entertainment column by Thursday. Your name spelled right, for once."
Tip your hat and head out.

content.dialogue.klieg-light-intro.hold-.en: "A closed mouth and a good instinct, that is rare on this street," he says, tapping the notebook shut. "I will hold it. But you owe me the first word when it is official, and I never forget a debt."
Shake on it and head out.

content.dialogue.klieg-light-intro.cool-.en: "Everybody's got something," he says, tipping his hat back with the pencil. "You know where the desk is."
Walk back out onto the Boulevard.

content.dialogue.klieg-light-intro.c2-ro.en: The newsman peers over a half-typed column, sleeves rolled, ink on his chin. "The gossip says you're in pictures now," he says. "Gossip is usually late. I'd like to be early."

content.dialogue.klieg-light-intro.c2-ni.en: "A first credit is a story," he says, rolling a sheet of copy paper out of his machine. "Not a big one. But I run small ones next to ads for toothpaste, and nobody reads the toothpaste. What I'd like is the first word, in your own words, in exchange for a column inch you can use." He eyes you. "Everyone in this business trades. I just prefer to be honest about the price."
Give him the first word on your Lookout. (-10 Energy)
Ask him to hold it for now. (-10 Energy)
Bargain him up to a fee for the first word. (-10 Energy)

The newsman stops typing. "I hear Monarch's publicity man has taken a shine to you," he says carefully. "Be careful whose favors you collect, friend. Not because anything is wrong with them. Because, in this town, the ones who give them have a very long memory." He rolls out his copy paper. "I'd still like the first word, if you're offering. Mine is cheaper, and it comes with fewer strings."
Give him the first word on your Lookout. (-10 Energy)
Ask him to hold it for now. (-10 Energy)
Bargain him up to a fee for the first word. (-10 Energy)

He types for a full minute without looking up, then tears the sheet free with a flourish. "'Newcomer wins the Lookout,' with your name spelled correctly, which I assure you is a courtesy." He pins it to the board behind his desk. "You gave me something. I won't forget it."
"Off the record." He lowers his pencil with visible reluctance, then smiles. "I admire that, even if my editor won't. I'll hold it. Come back when you have something you want printed."

"A fee, for a first word." He laughs, and then counts out three bills and some change anyway. "You've got the instincts of a publicist, and I mean that as a compliment, mostly. Here. Don't spend it all on hats."

content.dialogue.celestial-palace-lobby..en: House Manager

A silver-templed man in a maroon tailcoat straightens from the velvet rope and sweeps a white glove toward the ceiling. "Welcome to the Celestial Palace," he says. "The feature does not start until the evening show, but the lobby is always open to those who can appreciate it."
Take in the painted ceiling.
Ask what is playing tonight.
Ask for the seat he promised at the Tuesday matinee. (-10 Energy)
Step back out to the Boulevard.
House Manager

"Every star up there is gold leaf, set by hand," he says, with the pride of a man reciting a family history. "They say that if you stand under the sunburst long enough, the industry notices you. Mostly it gives you a stiff neck."
Ask what is playing tonight.
Rub your neck and head out.
House Manager
"Monarch's new swashbuckler, The Corsair's Daughter, opens next month," he says, tapping an empty poster frame with the brass flashlight. "Until then it is newsreels and a cartoon."
Mention your background-extra voucher.
Thank him and head out.
House Manager

"Row F, center, and not a word about the voucher," he murmurs, walking you down the aisle by the light of the brass flashlight. On the screen a cartoon mouse is dodging a piano. Around you, the whole audience is laughing at the same instant, and you find yourself studying exactly how they do it.
Settle in and enjoy the show.
House Manager

"A Monarch voucher?" He straightens further, if that is possible, and lowers his voice. "Crew and extras sit free at the Tuesday matinee, and nobody asks where you got the seat. Ask for me at the rope."
Promise to come by.
House Manager

The house manager has thrown the ballroom doors open, and somewhere behind him a trio is warming up. "The company of The Corsair's Daughter has the Palace tonight," he says, "and I have the honor of keeping order in it. I do hope you've brought your dancing shoes."
Step into the ballroom.
Talk about something else.
Step back outside.
House Manager

The ballroom is gold and low light and the bright chatter of a company at the end of a picture. The scene partner stands by the punch bowl in a silver dress, the leading man is trying not to look as though he is waiting for someone, the counter girl has come straight from her shift with a flower pinned to her apron, and the rival leans in the doorway with the air of someone who does not intend to dance. "There is time for exactly one dance before the band takes its break," the house manager murmurs at your shoulder. "Who is it to be?"
Ask the scene partner to dance. (-10 Energy)
Ask the counter girl to dance. (-10 Energy)
Ask the rival to dance. (-10 Energy)
Ask the leading man to dance. (-10 Energy)
Dance with no one in particular, and with everyone in turn. (-10 Energy)
Scene Partner

She takes your hand without a word, and the band, as if it had been waiting, slips into something slow. You dance with the careful, startled grace of two people who have rehearsed every beat of a scene and have just been told to forget it. "I hoped you'd ask," she says, very low. Her hand stays in yours a moment longer than the music needs.
Leave the ballroom, a little dazed.
Counter Girl

"Me?" she says, flushing to her hairline, and then, in a rush: "Well, I should hope so, I came all the way over here." The flower on her apron is slightly crushed, and she smells of coffee and lilac. She dances badly, and cheerfully, and without any of her usual jokes, and when the song ends she keeps hold of your sleeve. "That was swell," she says. "That was really swell."
Leave the ballroom, a little dazed.
Rival

"You're joking," she says, and when you aren't, she lifts her chin. "I'm leading." She does. She dances the way she does everything, as if the floor were a stage and every other couple a rival, and halfway through, the stiffness goes out of her shoulders, and for four bars she simply dances. "Don't tell anyone," she mutters. "It's a truce. Not a surrender."
Leave the ballroom, a little dazed.
Leading Man

"Oh, I should warn you," the leading man says, as he takes your hand, "I fall off things." He does not; he dances with a rider's balance, steady and careful and unexpectedly light, and when you tell him so, he flushes. "That's the nicest thing anyone's said to me this year." The music lingers, and so does he.
Leave the ballroom, a little dazed.
House Manager

You spend the evening wherever the music carries you: a waltz with the scene partner, a lindy hop with the counter girl, a tango with the rival that turns into a competition, and a clumsy turn about the floor with the leading man, who steps on your foot and apologizes four times. By the end, everyone is laughing. "A wise choice," the house manager says, passing you a glass of lemonade. "The evening is long, and the studio is longer."
Leave the ballroom, a little dazed.
